outcome: Nothing has happened to the planar statement since 26 January 2024: no proof, counterexample or new planar bound was found, and the best planar bound is still Xu's 2021 bound 1.393(|V|-1); the only in-window thrackle paper (arXiv 2506.11808, June 2025) disproves a genus-g analogue on orientable surfaces and restates the planar conjecture as open.
problem_asks: Part 1 (the whole statement): for every graph that has a thrackle drawing in the plane (a drawing in which every pair of edges meets exactly once, either at a shared endpoint or at a proper crossing), the number of edges m is at most the number of vertices n, i.e. m <= n for every thrackleable graph. There is one universal claim and no parameter. Equivalent form given by Wikipedia and Epoch: every thrackle is a pseudoforest. Context not asked for by the statement: the bound would be sharp, since every cycle of length at least five is thrackleable (Wikipedia, Mohar's problem page). The statement does not ask for the sharp constant, a classification, or a counterexample; a counterexample would be a thrackleable graph with m > n.

events.what_happened: Straight-line (linear) thrackles satisfy m <= n: Paul Erdos is credited in the Wikipedia Thrackle article with showing that for linear thrackles the edge count cannot exceed the vertex count, and a search excerpt of a secondary write-up places the argument in response to a 1934 Hopf-Pannwitz question on unit distances. Perles gave a later short proof (per the same excerpt). I could not establish the year or the venue of Erdos's argument from any source I opened, so the date is left null.
events.delivers: Restricted to straight-line thrackles (edges drawn as line segments): m <= n. This is the one case of the conjecture the sources describe as proved for a class of drawings by an early author.
events.remains: The conjecture for all thrackles, including curved edges; the statement's general m <= n.
events.directly_checkable: A straight-line thrackle is checkable by hand as a set of segments; the sources give no specific example.
events.doubts: Attribution conflicts: Wikipedia credits Erdos, while one search excerpt credits Woodall (1969/1971) with the straight-line case (see disputes). Date and venue not established.
events.direction: Consistent with the conjecture (proves the m <= n inequality for linear thrackles).
people: Micha Perles (later proof, per a search excerpt)

events.what_happened: D. R. Woodall, 'Thrackles and deadlock', in Combinatorial Mathematics and its Applications (Oxford conference, July 1969; volume published by Academic Press, 1971). Per Mohar's problem page and Wikipedia: every tree and every cycle of length at least 5 is thrackleable, and a minimal counterexample would be the one-point union of two even cycles (Woodall's paper itself was not opened; these are secondary citations). The conjecture is attributed to Conway in the late 1960s, and Woodall's paper is the standard early reference.
events.delivers: Structural partial results only: trees and cycles of length >= 5 are thrackleable (so the conjectured bound m <= n is attained there), and a counterexample, if one exists, must contain a one-point union of two even cycles. Gives no bound on edges for general thrackleable graphs.
events.remains: m <= n for all thrackleable graphs.
events.directly_checkable: The thrackle drawings of cycles of length at least 5 are checkable by hand; no specific drawing was read from the source.
events.direction: Consistent with the conjecture: exhibits thrackleable graphs with m <= n and restricts the shape of any counterexample.
events.object: Drawings showing that every tree and every cycle of length at least 5 is thrackleable (structural; no counterexample). Explicit or not is not stated in the secondary sources.

events.what_happened: J. Lovasz, J. Pach and M. Szegedy, 'On Conway's thrackle conjecture' (Discrete and Computational Geometry, 1997 per the Wikipedia citation). Per thrackle.org, the results are dated 1995: a bipartite thrackleable graph is planar (so it has a thrackle drawing only if planar), and every thrackleable graph on V vertices has at most 2V-3 edges. Mohar's problem page (dated August 1995, last edited February 2001) gives the 2V-3 bound as a personal communication from Szegedy. The 1997 journal paper was not opened.
events.revisions: Problem pages date the results to 1995; journal publication 1997 (per Wikipedia citation). The 1995 date is the earliest written appearance I found.
events.delivers: A linear upper bound: every thrackleable graph on n vertices has at most 2n-3 edges (so m <= 2n-3, not m <= n). Also: a bipartite thrackleable graph is planar.
events.remains: The gap from 2n-3 down to n: m <= n for all thrackleable graphs.

checked_by.who: Discrete and Computational Geometry (journal of record)
checked_by.what_they_did: Published the paper (per the Wikipedia citation). I did not open the publisher page, which was not reachable.

events.direction: Consistent with the conjecture; proves a linear (non-sharp) bound and a planarity statement for bipartite thrackles.

events.what_happened: G. Cairns and Y. Nikolayevsky, 'Bounds for generalized thrackles', Discrete and Computational Geometry 23(2) (2000), pp. 191-206 (DOI 10.1007/PL00009495). Later sources give the planar thrackle bound as m <= 3/2(n-1) (thrackle.org writes 1.5(V-1)); a search excerpt of the abstract reads '2/3(n-1)', which other sources treat as a typo. The paper also gives m <= 2n-2 for generalized thrackles (adjacent edges meet an even number of times, non-adjacent an odd number), and proposes the orientable genus-g analogue m <= n+2g, which was disproved in June 2025 (see that event). The Springer page was not reachable; the abstract was read only through search excerpts.
events.delivers: Planar thrackles: m <= 3/2(n-1) (as cited by later papers; the abstract as read through excerpts is garbled). Generalized thrackles in the plane: m <= 2n-2. Orientable surfaces of genus g: conjectured m <= n+2g (not established; disproved 2025).
events.remains: m <= n for thrackles in the plane; the gap between 3/2(n-1) and n.

checked_by.who: Discrete and Computational Geometry (journal of record)
checked_by.what_they_did: Published the paper (per DBLP and later citations). Full text not read.

events.doubts: The printed planar constant differs between the abstract excerpt (2/3(n-1)) and every later citation (3/2(n-1)); I treated 3/2 as the correct value but did not verify it against the paper.
events.direction: Consistent with the conjecture (upper bound, not sharp).

events.what_happened: R. Fulek and J. Pach, 'A computational approach to Conway's thrackle conjecture', arXiv:1002.3904 (posted 20 Feb 2010), published in Computational Geometry 44(6-7) (2011), pp. 345-355 (per thrackle.org). The arXiv abstract gives a finite algorithm, for each eps > 0, that decides whether t(n) < (1+eps)n for all n > 2, and an improved bound t(n) <= 167/117 n < 1.428n. Wikipedia paraphrases the algorithm as either improving the bound to (1+eps)n or disproving the conjecture; I did not see that second clause in the abstract.
events.revisions: arXiv v1 only (20 Feb 2010); journal version 2011 (per thrackle.org).
events.delivers: Planar upper bound t(n) <= 167/117 n (about 1.428n), valid for all thrackles. The finite algorithm reduces the question to a computation for each eps, which I did not see carried to a conclusion in the abstract.
events.remains: Whether t(n) = n for all n; the bound 1.428n is above the conjectured n.

checked_by.what_they_did: Published the paper (per thrackle.org citation). Journal page not read.

events.direction: Consistent with the conjecture: moves the planar bound, does not contradict it.

events.what_happened: J. Pach and E. Sterling, 'Conway's conjecture for monotone thrackles', American Mathematical Monthly 118(6) (2011), DOI 10.4169/amer.math.monthly.118.06.544. Wikipedia and a search excerpt state the conjecture holds for thrackles in which every edge is an x-monotone curve (each edge meets every vertical line at most once). The journal page was blocked (403) and the arXiv-hosted PDF was unreadable, so the statement rests on these secondary citations. Straight-line thrackles with no vertical edge are x-monotone (per the search excerpt).
events.revisions: A draft PDF at users.renyi.hu carries a 2009-style file name; its date could not be read. The 2011 date is the journal year.
events.delivers: The conjecture for x-monotone thrackles (every edge an x-monotone curve): m <= n in that class.
events.remains: The conjecture for thrackles whose edges are not all x-monotone.

checked_by.what_they_did: Published the paper (per DOI and Wikipedia citation). Full text not read.

events.direction: Consistent with the conjecture; proves it for a restricted class of drawings.

events.what_happened: G. Misereh and Y. Nikolayevsky, 'Thrackles containing a standard musquash', arXiv:1601.05562 (first posted 21 Jan 2016; one version), published in Australasian Journal of Combinatorics 70(2) (2018), pp. 168-184 (per search excerpt, journal page not opened). The abstract proves that a thrackle containing a standard musquash (a standard n-gonal thrackle) contains no other cycle of length 3 or 5. The abstract restates the conjecture and does not claim to settle it.
events.delivers: Structural: a thrackle containing a standard musquash has no 3-cycle and no 5-cycle besides possibly the musquash cycle itself (per abstract). Says nothing about the number of edges.
events.remains: The whole edge-count inequality m <= n.

checked_by.who: Australasian Journal of Combinatorics (journal of record)
checked_by.what_they_did: Published the paper (per search excerpt). Journal page not opened.

events.directly_checkable: A standard musquash is a constructible drawing (odd cycle, vertices on a circle, each joined to the vertex farthest from it); checkable by hand.
events.direction: Neutral structural result; does not cut against the conjecture.

events.what_happened: G. Misereh and Y. Nikolayevsky, 'Annular and pants thrackles', arXiv:1708.07351 (v1 24 Aug 2017; v2 31 Mar 2018; v3 22 May 2018, current). The authors prove Conway's conjecture for thrackle drawings all of whose vertices lie on the boundaries of at most d <= 3 connected components of the complement of the drawing, and characterise the d = 2 (annular) and d = 3 (pants) cases. A search excerpt of the PDF header gives acceptance in April 2018; the journal was not identified.
events.revisions: v1 24 Aug 2017; v2 31 Mar 2018; v3 22 May 2018 (per arXiv abstract page).
events.delivers: The conjecture (m <= n) for thrackle drawings in which every vertex lies on the boundary of at most three complementary domains. Restricted class: the boundary condition on vertices is an extra hypothesis, and the planar drawing is assumed to be a thrackle drawing as defined. Also descriptions of annular (d = 2) and pants (d = 3) thrackles.
events.remains: The conjecture for drawings with vertices on four or more complementary domains, and for general thrackles.
events.doubts: The only checking I found is by the authors (La Trobe University). No independent reading or journal identity was found in my searches, so the result has not been shown to have been checked by anyone outside the authors.
events.direction: Consistent with the conjecture; proves it for a restricted class.

events.what_happened: Yian Xu, M.Sc. thesis 'Generalized thrackles and graph embeddings' (Simon Fraser University, 2014, supervised by L. Goddyn), whose abstract (as a search excerpt gives it) states that by using discharging rules e <= 1.4n is shown for thrackles. Later sources cite this as Goddyn and Xu (2017), with 1.4n in some and 1.4n - 1.4 in another survey. The thesis was not opened; the statement rests on the search excerpt.
events.revisions: Cited as Goddyn and Xu (2017) by later sources; the thesis is dated 2014.
events.delivers: Planar thrackles: m <= 1.4n (approximately; one source gives 1.4n - 1.4).
events.doubts: Known only through a search excerpt of the abstract; the thesis was not read. The constant form differs between sources.
events.direction: Consistent with the conjecture; moves the planar bound.

events.what_happened: R. Fulek and J. Pach, 'Thrackles: An Improved Upper Bound', arXiv:1708.08037 (posted 27 Aug 2017; one version). The arXiv abstract states that any thrackle of n vertices has at most 1.3984n edges. Published in Graph Drawing 2017 (per the arXiv comments field) and in Discrete Applied Mathematics 259(4) (2019) per repository records found by search. The arXiv abstract also covers quasi-thrackles (max 3/2(n-1), tight for infinitely many n) per a search excerpt.
events.revisions: arXiv v1 only (27 Aug 2017); Graph Drawing 2017 proceedings; Discrete Applied Mathematics 2019.
events.delivers: Planar thrackles: m <= 1.3984n for every thrackle on n vertices (abstract). The quasi-thrackle result is a different class (not the conjecture).

checked_by.who: Graph Drawing 2017 programme committee and proceedings (Springer LNCS 10692)
checked_by.what_they_did: Accepted the paper for GD 2017 (per the arXiv comments field). The LNCS page was not opened.
Published the journal version in 2019 (per repository records found by search). Not opened.

events.direction: Consistent with the conjecture; moves the planar bound.

events.what_happened: B. Keszegh and D. Simon, 'Convex Hull Thrackles', arXiv:2307.03252 (posted 6 Jul 2023; one version). Defines convex hull thrackles, a generalisation of linear thrackles from segments to convex hulls of point subsets. Proves that in convex position the number of convex hulls is at most the number of vertices, notes a general construction with one more, and gives a general upper bound of twice the number of vertices. The paper says 'It is known that this conjecture holds for linear thrackles.' Published in Discrete Mathematics 349(3) in 2026 (per a repository record found by search; not opened).
events.revisions: arXiv v1 only (6 Jul 2023); Discrete Mathematics 349(3) 2026.
events.delivers: A generalisation, not the conjecture: convex hull thrackles, with a bound of the number of convex hulls by the number of vertices in convex position and by twice the number of vertices in general. It restates the linear case as known.
events.remains: The conjecture for thrackles with curved edges, and in fact all of the planar statement; this paper does not change it.

checked_by.what_they_did: Published the paper in 2026 (per a repository record found by search; not opened).

events.direction: Neutral for the conjecture: a neighbouring problem (convex hulls) with a different quantity.

events.what_happened: O. Aichholzer, L. Kleist, B. Klemz, F. Schroeder and B. Vogtenhuber, 'On the edge-vertex ratio of maximal thrackles', arXiv:1908.08857 (v1 23 Aug 2019; v2 17 Sep 2019), Graph Drawing 2019 (LNCS 11904, pp. 482-495 per search excerpt). Studies the minimum edge-vertex ratio of maximal thrackles (no edge can be added while remaining a thrackle). The arXiv abstract says the ratio can be arbitrarily small for maximal geometric and topological thrackles, arbitrarily close to 1/2 for geometric thrackles without isolated vertices, and gives a 5/6 family for topological thrackles without isolated vertices.
events.revisions: v1 23 Aug 2019; v2 17 Sep 2019 (per arXiv abstract page); GD 2019 proceedings.
events.delivers: Lower-end questions about maximal thrackles (minimum edge-vertex ratio), not the maximum number of edges. Does not bound the number of edges of a thrackle from above.
events.remains: The conjecture m <= n (an upper bound on edges of all thrackles) is untouched.

checked_by.who: Graph Drawing 2019 programme committee and proceedings (LNCS 11904)
checked_by.what_they_did: Accepted for GD 2019 (per search excerpt). LNCS page not opened.

events.directly_checkable: The 5/6 family is a specific family of topological thrackles; not checked by me.
events.doubts: The Graz institute page gives 4/5 for the topological case while the arXiv abstract gives 5/6; I followed the arXiv abstract. The discrepancy does not affect the conjecture.
events.direction: Neutral for the conjecture: a neighbouring quantity (minimum edge density of maximal thrackles).

events.what_happened: E. Ruiz-Vargas, A. Suk and G. Toth, 'Disjoint edges in topological graphs and the tangled-thrackle conjecture', arXiv:1406.2726 (June 2014; v2 Aug 2015 per search excerpt), published 2016 (per repository record). Proves the tangled-thrackle conjecture of Pach, Radoicic and Toth, a relaxed version in which two edges may also be tangent at a shared point, namely that such graphs have O(n) edges. This is a different problem from Conway's conjecture (the tangled version), and the paper was not opened.
events.revisions: arXiv v2 Aug 2015 (per search excerpt); published 2016 (per repository record).
events.delivers: A linear edge bound for tangled thrackles (a relaxed variant, a different problem): O(n) edges. Not about the planar thrackle conjecture.
events.remains: Conway's conjecture (m <= n for thrackles) is unaffected.
events.direction: Neutral: a neighbouring problem (tangled thrackles).

events.what_happened: Yian Xu, 'A New Upper Bound for Conway's Thrackles', Applied Mathematics and Computation 389 (2021), article 125573 (DOI 10.1016/j.amc.2020.125573). The abstract, as I read it on the ideas.repec mirror, states that |E| is no more than 1.393(|V|-1). Wikipedia states the current record as 1.393n, citing this paper. The 2025 arXiv paper (arXiv:2506.11808) states m <= 1.393n and attributes it to Xu [20], and says the conjecture 'remains open'. The current best planar bound is therefore this 2021 result.
events.revisions: Journal publication 2021; no earlier arXiv posting or preprint date found.
events.delivers: Planar thrackles: m <= 1.393(n-1) (abstract). Later sources restate this as m <= 1.393n, which is weaker by the n-1 term only.
events.remains: m <= n; the gap is about 39%.

checked_by.who: Applied Mathematics and Computation (journal of record, Elsevier)
checked_by.what_they_did: Published the paper (per the ideas.repec record, which I read). The Elsevier full text was not reachable.

events.doubts: The published abstract gives 1.393(|V|-1), but the 2025 paper and Wikipedia state 1.393n without the -1 term. I could only read the abstract, not the body, so whether the bound is 1.393(n-1) or 1.393n is not settled here.
events.direction: Consistent with the conjecture; moves the planar bound.

events.what_happened: C. Hernandez-Velez, J. Kyncl and G. Salazar, 'Thrackles on nonplanar surfaces', arXiv:2506.11808 (math.CO; submitted 13 Jun 2025; one version, v1). The abstract states: 'We disprove this conjecture', referring to Cairns and Nikolayevsky's conjecture that a thrackleable graph on an orientable surface S_g has m <= n+2g. It shows that for each g > 0 there is a connected graph with n vertices and 2n+2g-8 edges that can be thrackled on S_g, and that every connected graph thrackleable on S_g satisfies m <= 2n+4g-2. It also proves a similar result for nonorientable surfaces and gives genus bounds for K_{m,n} and K_n. The abstract also states: 'Conway's conjecture remains open; the best bound known is that m <= 1.393n.'
events.revisions: v1 only (per arXiv abstract page, opened).
events.delivers: A disproof of the genus-g analogue of the conjecture (m <= n+2g) for orientable surfaces S_g, g > 0, and of a nonorientable analogue. Scope is surfaces of positive genus, not the plane. It establishes nothing about m <= n for planar thrackles.
events.remains: The planar statement m <= n for thrackles in the plane: explicitly still open per the paper.
events.directly_checkable: The construction for each g > 0 (a graph with n vertices and 2n+2g-8 edges thrackled on S_g) is a specific drawing that could be checked by hand. I did not read the construction in the body of the paper, so I cannot say whether it is explicit.
events.direction: Cuts against the surface analogue of the conjecture (Cairns and Nikolayevsky's m <= n+2g), by exhibiting graphs above that bound on S_g. It does not cut against or for the planar conjecture, which the paper restates as open.
events.object: For each genus g > 0, a connected graph with n vertices and 2n+2g-8 edges that can be drawn as a thrackle on the orientable surface S_g (the family is described in the abstract; the construction is in the body, which I did not read). Its explicitness is not stated in the abstract.

events.what_happened: B. Keszegh, A. Suk, G. Tardos and J. Zeng, 'Unavoidable patterns and plane paths in dense topological graphs', arXiv:2512.04795 (submitted 4 Dec 2025; v2 24 Feb 2026), published in SoCG 2026 (LIPIcs.SoCG.2026.63). The paper's main results are on plane paths in dense simple topological graphs (for example O(n^(4/3)) edges for k = 3). Its introduction states: 'The famous thrackle conjecture of Conway states that a thrackle with n vertices has at most n edges.' The paper does not claim to resolve the conjecture and does not describe it as open. It also says 'we used a computer program to verify Lemma 15' in a proof, a conventional computer check.
events.revisions: v1 4 Dec 2025; v2 24 Feb 2026 (per arXiv abstract page); SoCG 2026 proceedings (per Dagstuhl record).
events.delivers: Establishes nothing about thrackles: a bound on plane paths in dense topological graphs. Restates the conjecture as background only.

checked_by.what_they_did: Accepted the paper for SoCG 2026 (per the Dagstuhl LIPIcs record).

events.direction: Neutral: a neighbouring problem; background mention of the conjecture as stated.

events.what_happened: Epoch AI lists 'Conway's Thrackle Conjecture' as a problem in FrontierMath: Open Problems, graph theory, status Unsolved, tags 'Construction - Finite' and 'Solid result'. The task asks for a counterexample: a graph with more edges than vertices that has a thrackle embedding, submitted as vertex coordinates and edge polylines. The page states that the main risk is that 'the conjecture is in fact true, in which case no counterexample exists'. No attempts, solvers or results are listed. The page carries no date; its footer reads '© 2026' and its citation gives an access date of 12 Oct 2026, which is later than the date of this run (11 Oct 2026). The date I give is inferred from the 2026 footer and from the open-problems pilot (27 Jan 2026), which does not name this problem.
events.revisions: Undated; the access date printed on the page is later than today.
events.delivers: Nothing: this is a benchmark task, not a mathematical result. It defines the task as finding a thrackle with more edges than vertices. Its definition says 'every edge crosses every other edge exactly once', which differs from the standard definition (edges sharing an endpoint meet there, not by crossing).
events.directly_checkable: A submitted counterexample would be checked by Epoch's verifier, which the page says tests that the embedding satisfies the edge crossing properties and rejects coincident polyline vertices. No counterexample is recorded.
events.doubts: The page's definition ('every edge crosses every other edge exactly once') does not match the standard thrackle definition, under which adjacent edges meet at their shared vertex. Which definition the verifier applies is not stated on the page. This is a scope issue for any future Epoch-recorded counterexample, not evidence about the conjecture.
events.direction: Frames the conjecture as one a counterexample would refute; no object reported.

disputes.summary: The straight-line (linear) case: Wikipedia attributes the proof to Paul Erdos. One search excerpt of a Woodall abstract says Woodall (1969/1971) showed the conjecture true for straight-line thrackles. Not resolved; Woodall's paper was not opened.
Xu (2021): the published abstract gives |E| <= 1.393(|V|-1); Wikipedia and the 2025 arXiv paper state m <= 1.393n.
Cairns and Nikolayevsky (2000): planar thrackle bound printed as 2/3(n-1) in an excerpt of the abstract, but cited everywhere else as 3/2(n-1) (thrackle.org writes 1.5(V-1)).
Goddyn and Xu's bound: dated 2014 (Xu's SFU M.Sc. thesis) by one source and 2017 (joint paper) by others; the constant is 1.4n in some sources and 1.4n - 1.4 in another.
Lovasz-Pach-Szegedy: dated 1995 by thrackle.org and Mohar's page, and 1997 by the Wikipedia citation (journal year).
Fulek-Pach (2017): 1.3984n in the arXiv abstract, and 1.398n in one search excerpt (same bound, different rounding).
Aichholzer et al. (2019): topological maximal thrackles without isolated vertices, edge-vertex ratio 5/6 in the arXiv abstract but 4/5 on the Graz institute page. The arXiv value is followed here.

Epoch's problem page defines a thrackle as a drawing in which 'every edge crosses every other edge exactly once', which does not match the standard definition (edges sharing an endpoint meet there). The verifier's convention is not stated.

summary: The planar statement (m <= n for every thrackleable graph) has no event in the window that changes it. The best planar bound is still Xu's 2021 result (Applied Mathematics and Computation 389, article 125573), whose abstract reads |E| <= 1.393(|V|-1); Wikipedia and the 2025 arXiv paper restate it as 1.393n. The one thrackle paper in the window, arXiv:2506.11808 (Hernandez-Velez, Kyncl and Salazar, submitted 13 June 2025), disproves a genus-g analogue of the conjecture for orientable surfaces (Cairns and Nikolayevsky's m <= n+2g, refuted by graphs with 2n+2g-8 edges on S_g), and its abstract says 'Conway's conjecture remains open'. Whether it bears on this bullet is a scope call: it answers the surface analogue of the statement, which section 2.1 excludes, but it sits on the same conjecture's history and is recorded in full in the event above and in competing_reading. Pre-window partial results are recorded as events: Erdos (straight-line case, undated in my sources), Woodall (1969, structural), Lovasz-Pach-Szegedy (2n-3 and planarity of bipartite thrackles, 1995/1997), Cairns-Nikolayevsky (3/2(n-1), 2000), Fulek-Pach (167/117 n, 2010; 1.3984n, 2017), Pach-Sterling (x-monotone case, 2011), Misereh-Nikolayevsky (at most three complementary domains, 2017), Goddyn-Xu (1.4n, 2014) and Xu (1.393(n-1), 2021). Neighbouring results are recorded as discarded events: Keszegh-Simon (convex hulls), Aichholzer et al. (minimum edge density of maximal thrackles), Ruiz-Vargas-Suk-Toth (tangled thrackles), Misereh-Nikolayevsky (musquash structure) and Keszegh-Suk-Tardos-Zeng (plane paths, SoCG 2026, which states the conjecture without comment). AI: no AI system is named in connection with the conjecture in any source I opened or searched. The Epoch FrontierMath Open Problems page lists it as a benchmark task asking for a counterexample, Unsolved, with no attempts recorded. Epoch's 27 January 2026 pilot post and its March 2026 first-AI-solution post do not mention thrackles, and the Epoch index shows no thrackle status change. Two AI-and-proof stories that surfaced in search concern other problems (a cycle double cover claim, relayed secondhand, and a Lean attempt on a Conway refinement conjecture). Close calls: (i) whether the 2025 surfaces paper counts as an event on this bullet, since it refutes a conjecture of the same shape and mentions Conway's conjecture; (ii) whether the Xu bound is 1.393(n-1) or 1.393n; (iii) the Erdos linear-case date and attribution against Woodall's. Several full texts (Springer, Taylor and Francis 403, Elsevier redirect, binary PDFs) were not readable, so the 2000, 2011 and 2021 journal statements rest on secondary citations and abstracts.
competing_reading: Count the 2025 surfaces paper, and the Epoch benchmark, as in-window events on this bullet. The surfaces result refutes Cairns and Nikolayevsky's own generalisation of Conway's bound, uses the same vocabulary, and restates the planar conjecture as open; read that way, the event is a disproof of an analogue of the problem, which the scope test in the instructions excludes. The Epoch page is an AI-oriented framing of the same question, which a reader might count as AI attention, but it reports no result. A reader who takes the Xu bound as 1.393n and dates it from the Wikipedia restatement would place the bound in the window, but its publication is in 2021.
what_would_settle_it: For a no-change verdict on the planar statement: a date-sorted arXiv search for 'thrackle' through October 2026 (not possible from this search tool), the citing-papers list for Xu 2021 and Fulek-Pach 2017, and the revision history or attempts log of the Epoch thrackle page. For the constant and the -1 term: the Elsevier full text of Xu 2021 and the Springer full text of Cairns-Nikolayevsky 2000. For a change: a dated preprint proving m <= n, or a thrackleable graph with m > n, with a named expert check or a Lean build with no sorry.

judgement.why: The statement is the single planar claim m <= n for thrackles. All bound-moving and case-settling events (linear, x-monotone, three-domain cases; 2n-3, 3/2(n-1), 1.428n, 1.4n, 1.3984n, 1.393(n-1)) predate January 2024, and none determines the quantity. The only post-snapshot mathematics, the 2025 surfaces paper, refutes Cairns-Nikolayevsky's genus-g analogue m <= n+2g, which is a changed question; its own abstract says Conway's conjecture remains open, so it is a variant with no object bearing on the planar statement. The SoCG 2026 paper only mentions the conjecture, and the Epoch page is a benchmark. Woodall and the musquash paper give structural facts without a bound or a settled class, so none. The Erdos linear case has no date but is clearly pre-snapshot (early author, later proof by Perles, cited as known in 2023), so false rather than null. No AI system did any mathematics in any event.
judgement.doubts: Annular/pants case marked unreviewed because the journal is unidentified. Erdos vs Woodall priority for the linear case unresolved. Xu's bound is 1.393(n-1) or 1.393n; this doesn't affect any answer.
